definition.text: Ambiguity aversion is a preference for risks whose odds are known over risks whose odds are unknown.

facts.text: It was first shown by the Ellsberg paradox: people prefer betting on an urn of 50 red and 50 black balls over one of 100 balls in an unknown mix.
Risk aversion concerns a gamble against its expected value when odds are known; ambiguity aversion concerns known odds against unknown odds.
Unlike risk aversion, mainly put down to diminishing marginal utility, ambiguity aversion has no widely accepted main cause.
It has been used to explain incomplete contracts, stock-market volatility and selective abstention in elections.
Greater ambiguity aversion raises demand for insurance, as people dislike unknown events affecting their lives and property.
Experiments suggest attitudes to ambiguity depend on context, so a measure from one setting may not predict behaviour in another.

definition.text: Maxmin expected utility is a model in which a decision-maker holds several possible probability beliefs and picks the option whose worst-case expected utility is highest.

facts.text: Gilboa and Schmeidler proposed it in 1989 as an axiomatic account of ambiguity aversion.
Someone who thinks the chance of red in the unknown Ellsberg urn lies between 0.4 and 0.6 would, under maxmin, prefer to bet on the known urn.
Schmeidler's Choquet expected utility model, which allows non-additive probabilities, includes maxmin as a special case.
A max-min social welfare function reflects an extreme uncertainty aversion by society, caring only about the worst-off.

definition.text: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals, usually for a limited term.

facts.text: Life insurers commonly sell annuities: a person pays a lump sum or premiums in return for regular income, often for retirement.
Everyday examples include regular savings deposits, monthly mortgage payments, insurance premiums and pension payments.
Its value is expressed as a present or future value by discounting or accumulating the payments at a stated interest rate.
An annuity-immediate pays at the end of each period, like mortgage repayments; an annuity-due pays at the start, like rent.
An annuity that continues indefinitely is a perpetuity.
In medieval and early modern Europe, annuities let lenders provide credit where direct interest-bearing loans were restricted.
By the 16th and 17th centuries governments in the Dutch Republic, France and England sold annuities to raise money.

definition.text: A life annuity pays for as long as one or more named people stay alive, so the number of payments is uncertain.

facts.text: Pensions paying a regular income for life are life annuities.
By contrast, an annuity certain pays for a fixed period whatever happens to anyone's survival.
Valuing a life annuity accounts for mortality as well as interest: its actuarial present value is the expected value of the discounted payments.
Halley's 1693 work showed how a life table built from mortality data could be used to price annuities.

definition.text: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original sum and on interest already added to it.

facts.text: It differs from simple interest, where past interest is not added to the principal.
$1,000 at 5% a year grows to $1,050 after one year and $1,102.50 after two, because the second year's interest is on the new total.
The compounding frequency can be yearly, monthly, daily, continuous or not at all until maturity.
Compound interest at a constant rate gives exponential growth of capital.
Luca Pacioli's Rule of 72 (1494) says the years for money to double is roughly 72 divided by the interest rate.
Lenders charging compound interest were once condemned as the worst kind of usury under Roman law.
Garrett Hardin argued any economy based on long-term compound interest must fail, since exponential growth is impossible on a finite planet.

definition.text: Continuous compounding is the limit reached when interest is compounded ever more often, with the compounding period shrinking towards zero.

facts.text: Under continuous compounding the effective annual rate approaches an upper limit of e^r − 1.
The continuously compounded rate is called the force of interest.
It is often used because it is mathematically simpler, for example when valuing financial derivatives.
Jacob Bernoulli discovered the constant e in 1683 by studying a compound interest question.

definition.text: The effective annual rate is the total interest payable over one year divided by the principal, putting rates with different compounding on a common footing.

facts.text: Many countries require lenders and banks to disclose this annual compound rate so consumers can compare products fairly.
It goes by names such as annual equivalent rate (AER), effective annual percentage rate and annual percentage yield.
Bonds paying interest twice a year have a yearly compounded rate higher than their quoted rate.
